    New research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.

    Recent findings suggest that according to the report, which was released by the university’s researchers Thursday, more than a third of civil suits filed in Santa Clara County, California, and San Francisco County this year show signs of AI use. The researchers noted that this doesn’t include debt collection cases.

    It has been revealed that among other findings, Stanford’s researchers noted that pro se litigants had higher AI adoption rates. In Santa Clara County, the share of self-represented complaints that showed signs of AI use increased from 19% in 2024 to 72% in 2026. Meanwhile, the share of attorney-filed complaints increased from 5% to 34% during this period.

    It has been revealed that researchers also found that the use of AI varies by case type, with employment and business complaints in California showing the highest rates. They remarked AI use also varies throughout court filings, with more appearances in the statement of facts and causes of actions sections.

    “The sharp rise we document here corroborates that AI in the law is a question of how, not whether,” Stanford’s researchers wrote in the report.

    • “The landmark International Court of Justice ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, (The Hague) – The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is a historic milestone in their long quest for justice, Human Rights Watch said today. On November 19, 2026, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations,” carried out by Myanmar’s military.

    It has been revealed that in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Genocide Convention), the court ruled for Gambia, with a nine to six vote by the judges, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. This is the first time that the ICJ found a country responsible for committing genocide. The court also found that Myanmar violated other obligations under the Genocide Convention, including the obligations to punish those responsible for genocide and to prevent genocide. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

    “The landmark International Court of Justice ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide and other grave crimes across the world in their own search for justice.”.

    In a recent development, in August 2017, Myanmar’s security forces began a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In November 2019, Gambia filed a case before the ICJ alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention. This was also the first time that a country without any direct connection to the alleged crimes used its membership in the Genocide Convention to bring a case before the ICJ.

    Sources indicate that the ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, adjudicating disputes between states and issuing advisory opinions on international law. It consists of 15 judges elected by the UN General Assembly and Security Council for nine-year terms.

    In its ruling, the ICJ found that the evidence before it established that Myanmar’s security forces, and other state organs, intentionally committed the genocidal acts of killing, causing serious bodily or mental harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births against the Rohingya.

    Considering the totality of the evidence, the court concluded that Myanmar committed these acts with the requisite genocidal intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population of Myanmar. To reach this conclusion, it considered an array of relevant factors, including the general context, the selective targeting of the Rohingya, acts that violated the foundations of the Rohingya group, such as sexual violence and targeting children, and the systematic nature of Myanmar’s actions.

    Industry observers note that based on these factors, the court found that Myanmar’s genocidal intent was “the only reasonable inference” that could be drawn from the evidence before it. The judges rejected the possibility that other alternative intents, such as to carry out counterinsurgency operations or to forcibly displace the Rohingya, could reasonably explain Myanmar’s conduct.

    Recent findings suggest that in light of its findings, the court ordered Myanmar to cease its ongoing violations of the Genocide Convention, including its failure to enact legislation to give effect to the convention and its failure to investigate, prosecute, and punish genocide. It found that Myanmar needs to provide assurances of non-repetition and is obliged to prevent similar violations in the future.

    The court also established that Gambia was entitled to seek reparations on behalf of Rohingya victims and ordered Myanmar to provide them. These include forms of restitution such as allowing and facilitating the safe, voluntary and dignified return of the Rohingya to their place of residence, and the reunification of displaced families. Whenever restitution is materially impossible, the court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations in the form of compensation.

    The court’s reasoning in this case is expected to have a profound impact on other pending cases before the ICJ regarding alleged violations of the Genocide Convention. This includes the case filed by South Africa against Israel in December 2023.

    Prior to the Myanmar judgment, US officials sought to pressure the ICJ and its judges with regard to the legal threshold for genocide. The US government has already sanctioned the International Criminal Court and several of its officials in an effort to shield senior US and Israeli officials from facing serious crimes charges before the court.

    In February 2021, following the November 2020 Myanmar elections won by Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy, the then-commander-in-chief, Sr. Gen. Min Aung Hlaing, led a military coup that overthrew the civilian government. More than five years later, Myanmar’s military junta continues to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity throughout the country. Min Aung Hlaing installed himself as president through fraudulent elections in December 2025 and January 2026.

    In a recent development, in Rakhine State since late 2023, Rohingya civilians have been caught in the hostilities between the junta and ethnic Arakan Army forces. Both parties have carried out grave abuses, including extrajudicial killings, widespread arson, and unlawful recruitment. The Myanmar military continues to commit war crimes against the Rohingya and the crimes against humanity of apartheid, persecution, and deprivation of liberty. The Arakan Army, which now controls most of Rakhine State, has tightened repression of the Rohingya, including forced labor and arbitrary detention, and has committed grave violations of the laws of war amounting to war crimes.

    ICJ judgments are legally binding on the parties to the case. If one party considers that the other has failed to comply with the court’s ruling, it may turn to the Security Council, which can “make recommendations or decide upon measures to be taken to give effect to the judgment.” The Security Council has never acted upon this discretionary power.

    It has been revealed that the UN General Assembly can galvanize political support to enforce ICJ judgments by adopting resolutions calling for compliance. Individual countries can also influence compliance through their bilateral engagement with the relevant party.

    Industry observers note that eleven countries that are parties to the Genocide Convention intervened in Gambia’s case on limited concerns relating to the construction of the convention. The court’s interpretation of the convention on these issues becomes legally binding for them.

    The ICJ ruling is a clear reminder of the importance of independent judicial institutions in upholding international law, Human Rights Watch said.

    Recent findings suggest that “Myanmar should swiftly comply with the World court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya,” Vignoli said. “Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The United States has recently made a concerted effort to water down draft resolutions at the United Nations that reference the rights of women and girls, sexual orientation and gender identity, and the International Criminal Court (ICC).

    The US efforts at the General Assembly’s Third Committee, which focuses on human rights, highlight the Trump administration’s positioning as an outlier among established democracies as it picks and chooses among universal human rights.

    Unlike in the UN Security Council, where the US and the other four permanent members have a veto and the US has successfully struck out language on the ICC, gender, and other topics — no single country can block General Assembly resolutions.

    At the Third Committee, the US targeted language in draft resolutions referencing sexual and reproductive rights for women and girls. For resolutions on violence against women and girls and trafficking in women and girls, the US proposed adding “in accordance with national laws” after such references. The proposed amendments reflect the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle internationally protected reproductive rights.

    Recent findings suggest that the US has not been acting alone. Russia proposed deleting an ICC reference from the resolution on trafficking in women and girls. Egypt submitted similar amendments to the resolution on violence against women and girls and sought to remove a reference to “sexual orientation and gender identity” from a resolution on extrajudicial executions.

    UN member countries rejected the amendments and adopted the resolutions.

    The US also voted against a resolution supporting human rights defenders because it included references to gender and reproductive rights. It abstained on human rights resolutions it traditionally supports on North Korea, Myanmar, and Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia because of ICC references. Those resolutions also passed.

    According to recent reports, the Trump administration’s assault on the international human rights system has not been limited to UN resolutions. It has imposed sanctions on ICC judges, prosecutors, nongovernmental groups, a UN human rights expert, and the court itself. It has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick” to prevent investigations of US and Israeli officials.

    Industry observers note that it’s heartening that these attempts by the US and others to undermine human rights and international accountability have failed so far. But UN member countries need to work together to resist future efforts to weaken human rights norms and international justice.

    #112954. Breaking: 5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1071 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: 5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, you expect danger in the city.
    • Recent findings suggest that there’s plenty of menace in small places.
    • I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, you expect danger in the city. Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living. Country intelligence has no succinct adjectives. Country-strong, that’s a thing. But, country-wise? More often than not, there is a misconception that life in the hinterlands will dull your edge, diminish your reflexes, lull you into a false sense of security.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s plenty of menace in small places. In towns with no interstate ramp, nameless desert stops with no cell phone service, a desperate farm community surrounded by an ocean of corn.

    I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors. These don’t have to be set in the South—mine are—but they can happen anywhere. Maybe it’s Southern noir when done south of the Mason-Dixon line. Rural noir is a good name, and throws its arms around the whole genre, but it’s a mouthful. It comes out sounding slurry, even when I’m sober, and might not come out at all if I’ve had a cocktail. This subgenre of crime fiction goes by many names. I wish I could just tell people I wrote Southerns and have them understand—the way most people understand the Western. Till then, here are five of my favorite examples of novels that take place out past the last lights of town.

    Crucial note: I had to leave out a lot of authors I adore and beg you to read anything and everything by the following for outstanding examples of small-town, insular, tight-nit, and Sun-Belt crime: Flannery O’Connor, S.A. Cosby, Carson McCullers, Henry Wise, Attica Locke, Dennis Lehane, Megan Abbott, Ivy Pochoda, and Elmore Leonard. Please find them.

    Daniel Woodrell is incredible. I love every word he has ever written but Tomato Red is my favorite. It opens with a gorgeous run-on sentence that’s almost three hundred words long and, after reading it, it’s almost impossible not to collapse and read the whole book in one sitting. The novel’s hapless anti-hero, Sammy Barlach—recently fired from a dog food factory and fresh off a speed-fueled burglary attempt—throws in with siblings Jason and Jamalee Merridew. Jason, a local object of female obsession, and his sister Jamalee want to weaponize Jason’s beauty, blackmail wealthy woman, and get them both out of Venus Holler. Sammy hitches his wagon to the Merridew’s scheme. But for Jason, a gay man in the hills and hollows of the Ozarks, choosing to live an authentic life proves to me more dangerous than one of crime.

    One of my favorite sayings from Tod Goldberg is that he writes about bad people doing terrible things to even worse people. In The Low Desert, he demonstrates this across twelve sometimes-connected stories set on the outskirts of California and Nevada. There are lonely deserts, fading resort towns, lost highways. Each story is a banger, but the fact that Goon Number Four isn’t your favorite TV show of the last decade is a miscarriage of justice. A story about a hired gun who enrolls in a community college, seeking to be rid of the life, only to find exploitation waiting in the halls of normalcy. The Low Desert has something I have never been able to fully articulate—feeling more like a great album, than the seminal work of crime fiction it is.

    A personal favorite, Thompson’s Pop. 1280 is a novel that perfectly balances menace and comedy. Nick Corey, a terrible sheriff, oversees the 1280 souls of Potts County, Texas. Many of Nick’s constituents don’t want a sheriff, prefer to skirt the law, and tolerate him because he is pathologically shiftless. Our sheriff eats five meals a day, sleeps with any woman who’s up for it, sees murder as the only option rather than a last resort, and will do anything to keep his job. Not because he is ambitious, but because being sheriff allows him to do almost nothing. But, on the precipice of a difficult reelection, he reluctantly springs into action. Through the ensuing morass, Nick confronts sassy pimps, his pushy wife and her brother, his mistress and her husband, the town as whole, and the very concept of righteousness. Corey is a man who seems dumb, but isn’t. Someone dangerous and ruthless in the most peculiar and befuddling ways.

    Cormac McCarthy, No Country for Old Men.

    Cormac McCarthy’s most accessible novel. It is a literary crime novel that dissects the corrosive effects of money, heightened to break-neck entertainment by the inclusion of one of fiction’s most unforgettable bad dudes. In many ways, this is Anton Chigurh’s book the way Jaws belongs to the shark. Chigurh, a relentless hitman who’s as dangerous to his employers as he is to his targets, is evil with biblical scope. Ed-Tom Bell is a good man fading. A sheriff having and existential crisis, struggling to adapt to the requirements of his calling in a world where criminality has moved past opportunism and into something inconceivable. Throw in Llewelyn Moss, a Vietnam vet who stumbles across two million dollars after a drug deal goes wrong, and you’re in for a ride. When Chigurh’s tide of malevolence come in. One man tries to stem it, the other retreats. Fates are decided by the flip of a coin.

    Frank Bill, Crimes in Southern Indiana.

    Frank Bill’s debut, Crimes in Southern Indiana, is a cold look at a brutal version of Indiana that exists off the interstates. Southern Indiana is an anomaly—not quite the South, not quite the Midwest. Claimed by none—like the folks Bill writes about. He drops seventeen stories about this distinct region across two hundred and seventy pages in an achingly authentic voice. He can do more damage in ten pages than most other savvy word-geeks could with a lifetime supply of paper. The Penance of Scoot McCutchen will wreck you. I think about it all the time.

    According to recent reports, ty Landers holds an MFA in Creative Writing and Writing for the Performing Arts from the University of California, Riverside. Born and raised in Alabama, he spent more than twenty years in Nashville, Tennessee, before moving to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with his wife and sons. His debut novel BABY QUEEN, out on November 17, 2026, is being adapted by HBO. For more on Ty Landers, visit: https://www.tylandersfiction.com/.

    #112952. The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2709 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.
    • Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.
    • Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I promptly moved into the world of e-discovery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 10:47 am CST.

    Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

    Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I promptly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

    Satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software company, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

    Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each upcoming matter at the outset?

    Industry observers note that chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of fresh datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material concerns in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or issue. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

    Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

    Satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every newly introduced tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

    Recent findings suggest that ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

    According to recent reports, chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our new law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

    Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

    Satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

    Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

    Industry observers note that chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same strategy from the outset.

    Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

    According to recent reports, satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client says it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”.

    Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

    In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati noted earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

    Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

    Satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

    Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

    In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely important, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

    Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

    Satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be stated in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

    Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

    According to recent reports, chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

    Listen to the complete interview at Reinventing Professionals.

    Ari Kaplan regularly interviews leaders in the legal industry and in the broader professional services community to share perspective, highlight transformative change and introduce new technology at his blog and on Apple Podcasts.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1005 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media.
    • Sources indicate that on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state.
    • “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media. Let alone the international news media. But during the traditionally slow Christmas holiday, when even serious outlets stoop to tracking Santa’s progress across the northern hemisphere and presenting expert commentary on decorations at the White House, the story about the bodies found in the backwoods of the Pacific Northwest arrived like a Christmas gift from News Kringle.

    Sources indicate that on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state. After a three-day search that involved more than sixty volunteers from two states, dogs, drones, and helicopters working through harsh terrain, icy conditions, and a snowstorm, their frozen bodies were recovered. On December 28, Portland’s CBS television affiliate KOIN 6 was among the first to pick up the story.

    “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.

    According to recent reports, did someone say Sasquatch? Every editor in the world knew clickbait when they saw it. Within days, near-identical headlines appeared around the world, backed by the biggest names in news.

    CNN: 2 Oregon men die from exposure in a forest after they went out to look for Sasquatch.

    Fox News: 2 dead after search for Sasquatch in Washington national forest.

    NPR: 2 men were found dead from exposure after looking for Sasquatch.

    BBC: Two men found dead while searching for Bigfoot.

    Nine News Australia: Two men found dead in US after going on Christmas Eve hunt for Bigfoot.

    Hundreds, perhaps thousands, jumped in. The Associated Press. MSN. CBS News. HuffPost. Newsweek. Today. Yahoo News. USA Today. Newly introduced York Post. Los Angeles Times. San Francisco Chronicle. The Times. Daily Mail.

    In a recent development, the story was such a surefire traffic pusher that even specialized outlets ran with it. People. Sports Illustrated. AccuWeather. The celebrity and entertainment website TooFab. Spain’s national sports tabloid Marca. New Zealand’s Stuff. Taiwanese tabloid CTWant. The massively popular 52hrtt, a Chinese-language website that serves the global Chinese diaspora.

    There was no video, so each outlet looped the same images from a package of photos released by the Skamania County 23 sasquatch country Sheriff’s Office: four SAR volunteers on a snow-covered trail carrying an extension ladder through the forest; six volunteers in safety-orange jackets and helmets, one pointing a finger into the woods, using an extension ladder laid on the ground to cross a stream; a guy on hands and knees crawling across the ladder over a stream; a group of seven searchers using downed logs to cross a stream; and a Coast Guard helicopter hovering above an opening in the forest canopy.

    According to recent reports, in a digitally powered echo chamber, local, regional, national, and international outlets repeated the story almost word for word. All the way across the continent, News Center Maine television led its December 30 national news roundup in typical fashion:.

    Sources indicate that we’ll start in Washington state. Two men were found dead there after going on a search for Bigfoot. They went out on their search a few days before Christmas Eve. When they didn’t return, family members contacted police. They were found after a three-day search. Local authorities there say it seems as though they likely died of exposure because of the weather conditions at the time and not being prepared.

    According to recent reports, sasquatch hunters. Christmas search. Poorly prepared. Died of exposure. That was all anyone seemed to know.

    Industry observers note that in fact, those elementary pieces of the story were all anyone in the news media actually did know. As even a cursory examination of the torrent of articles and broadcasts about the two bodies found in the forest revealed, the stories were noteworthy mostly for their striking uniformity and lack of information. But something about the story wasn’t right. Something didn’t add up.

    In a recent development, the rule that credible journalists are meant to follow is that the details in a story must support its headline—particularly if that headline makes an audacious claim. Two guys froze to death while looking for Bigfoot? Wow. Bring on the details.

    But that was the thing about the story of the Christmas Sasquatch hunters. After the stun-gun heds and ledes, there were no details about the supposed Sasquatch hunt. Not scant details. Not vague details. No details whatsoever. As if by mandate, every outlet that picked up the story made sure to include Sasquatch in its headline and opening grab. Then they dropped the Bigfoot angle altogether.

    It has been revealed that how long had the men been out looking for Sasquatch? Did they have a track record as Sasquatch hunters? Were they carrying special equipment, such as video cameras, long-range microphones, or telephoto lenses? If they were out searching for Sasquatch in rugged terrain and winter conditions, why were they so ill prepared?

    On these and other questions related to the Sasquatch hunt teased in the headlines, every story was the same—strangely mute.

    Excerpted from Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the New American Wilderness by Chuck Thompson via Counterpoint Press.

    In a recent development, chuck Thompson is the longtime editor of Columbia Insight, an award-winning environmental and outdoor news website based in Hood River, Oregon, just across the Columbia River from Skamania County and the Gifford Pinchot National Forest. A former executive producer with CNN.com, deputy editor of Men’s Journal, and Outside magazine contributor, he’s the author The Status Revolution: The Improbable Story of How the Lowbrow Became the Highbrow; the widely reviewed political screed Better Off Without ’Em: A Northern Manifesto for Southern Secession; the acclaimed travel memoir Smile When You’re Lying: Confessions of a Rogue Travel Writer; and Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the Upcoming American Wilderness.

    #112950. 5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1160 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted.
    • But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers.
    • Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted. It’s my eighth book. With each one I’ve taken a bigger, bolder, and yes, a more unhinged swing. And I’m not alone. There is a rabid pack of unhinged thriller writers out there, and we’re only getting more bananas.

    But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers. In fact, I’ve found it incredibly hard to whittle this list down to just five. This list bounces between the new, the nearly new and the really rather old.

    Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

    One of those novels so powerful that it becomes a conceptual byword (by-phrase?) used even by people who have never read it. Published in 1886 and so brisk it’s actually a novella, this unflinching gothic masterpiece still holds its own in 2026.

    There is almost as much mythology about the writing of the book as is contained in its pages. Stevenson claimed that it sprang from a wild nightmare that contained three scenes and the central idea, “of a voluntary change becoming involuntary.” His step-son claimed it was written in a three-day fit of pique. His wife claimed that Stephenson burned the first version after she suggested he was writing an allegory, which riled him up before he realized he agreed, and then started again.

    Stephenson’s health at the time was dire, he was on medication to stop his lungs hemorrhaging, which could have stimulated the originating nightmare. According to some rumors he was also taking cocaine, which could also explain the mad work rate and agitation….

    If you haven’t read it recently (or perhaps ever), you may raise an eyebrow at its inclusion in a list of thrillers but it more than earns its place.

    It has been revealed that we have unreliable characters, memory blackouts, dual personalities and a race to stop a killer. And it’s actually, I would argue, a speculative thriller given that the whole problem starts with Dr Jekyll experimenting to create a serum that can overcome the dark parts of his personality. Instead, the serum splits him into two—the good Dr Jekyll, and the evil Mr Hyde.

    Sarah Pinborough, Behind Her Eyes.

    It has been revealed that I know this came out nearly ten years ago but I’m still agape at its twists. Sarah Pinborough tore up the rule book with this one, and proved that you could still find fresh ways to shock a savvy audience of thriller readers.

    According to recent reports, if you’ve not read it, I don’t want to give anything away but what starts as a tense psychological thriller about a single mum having an affair with her boss while forming a close friendship with the boss’s wife, soon takes a hard swerve into lucid dreaming, astral projection and a past timeline exploring trauma and mental illness. And if that sounds heavy and gloomy, I’m doing it a massive disservice because it is an absolute rollercoaster.

    The ending was so WILD that it was a key part of the marketing, with the hashtag #WTFthatending spreading through Book Twitter (this was 2017, after all…).

    Lisa Jewell, None Of This Is True.

    According to recent reports, as a long-term fan, I loved watching the queen of women’s fiction become the doyenne of domestic suspense before winding her way down an ever-darker garden path. But Lisa Jewell’s 2023 novel, None Of This Is True, was a real escalation.

    It has been revealed that A fever dream of lies, paranoia and platonic limerence. Alix is a successful true crime podcaster who meets her “birthday twin,” Josie, an unassuming local woman born on the same day but whose life is very different.

    According to recent reports, they both have secrets, of course, which I’m loathe to give away but the novel is unflinching around dark topics like grooming, alcoholism and family dysfunction. For all its sucker punches (and the twists are *brain exploding emoji*) this is a nuanced and heartfelt exploration of the stories we tell ourselves in order to survive.

    In a recent development, if you were an unemployed gambling addict unable to pay your debts and whose loved ones were being threatened by the Yakuza, you’d take the first well-paid job that comes your way too, right? In this case, as a private chef to a reclusive billionaire in remote Japan.

    Soon, protagonist Ed is somewhat learning on the job in the best kitchen money can buy at the heart of an enormous mansion, with an endless supply of whatever ingredients the esoteric tastes of his boss desires….

    It’s been likened to Butter by Asako Yuzuki and there are overlaps in themes of greed, obsession and—of course—murder, but while Butter is a slow burn, Greedy is a runaway train. Messy, freaky and eye wateringly gory. I mean all those things as compliments!

    Fiona Cummins, Serial Killer Survivors Club.

    While 1980s teenager Robyn reels from the discovery that her father was a serial killer, her life is made infinitely worse by community ostracism and judgement.

    Recent findings suggest that an experimental therapy group for the familial survivors of murderers changes her life, finally giving her the acceptance and friendship she has always craved. But when one of her latest friends disappears in a town where three other young women are already missing, Robyn and her found-family risk everything to find them. After all, with their intimate knowledge of killers, the Serial Killer Survivors Club are the best hope these missing women have….

    I pat myself on the back for my ability to predict twists but this one spun me for a total loop. I was lucky enough to grab an advanced readers copy of this, which will be published next year in the UK and US. I highly recommend pre-ordering.

    My own unhinged thriller, The Sleeper, follows librarian Maya who falls asleep on a sleeper train and wakes up in a version of the world where history has changed overnight, her own life has been erased and nobody remembers her.

    Recent findings suggest that and the version of Britain she’s now living in? Just saying the wrong things can put you in the crosshairs of the state. Which is a massive problem for Maya, who in her bewilderment, has asked way too many questions already….

    It has been revealed that holly Seddon is the author of several thrillers, including the international bestseller Try Not to Breathe, The Hit List, and 59 Minutes. After growing up in the English countryside obsessed with music and books, Holly worked in London as a journalist and editor. After several years in Amsterdam, she now lives in Kent with her family and writes full time. Find out more at HollySeddon.com.

    #112949. Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2209 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, tuscany, 1972.
    • Recent findings suggest that when Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray.
    • Sources indicate that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful new novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, tuscany, 1972. Bardo Sacchetti has the people of the Val di Cornia wrapped around his little finger. Thanks to him and his band of tomb raiders, locals in the impoverished region can now buy fridges for their homes or give their kids an education. He asks for nothing in return except for gratitude.

    Recent findings suggest that when Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray. Former alliances fall apart and Bardo’s empire looks like it might be destroyed by violence. Veleno has some massive decisions to make.

    Sources indicate that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful new novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis. The story unfolds from their perspectives.

    Recent findings suggest that I sent written questions to Naspini, and Edoardo Andreoni translated his written responses from Italian into English. The interview has been edited for length.

    Radha Vatsal: Let’s start with some background. Tuscany, where the novel takes place, seems to be littered with antiquities. Is this more the case in Tuscany than in other parts of Italy? Can you describe some of the types of antiquities that have been found there in recent years?

    Sacha Naspini: Actually, that’s true of pretty much all of Italy. It’s a country where history has accumulated over millennia, layer upon layer. Here, even a routine excavation can turn into an archaeological discovery.

    It has been revealed that tuscany is no exception. In fact, it’s one of the regions where this historical layering is particularly evident, largely thanks to the Etruscan civilization, which preceded Roman rule. Discoveries are still being made today. Take the recent finds at San Casciano dei Bagni, near Siena: extraordinary bronzes, along with coins, crowns, jewelry, votive arms and heads….

    As for The Witch’s Mouth, the novel is set in a specific part of Tuscany, the Val di Cornia. It’s an area I know well, one that plays an important role in the fictional universe of some of my novels. This was once home to Populonia, one of the most important Etruscan cities and the only one built directly on the coast. In the Gulf of Baratti, you can visit Etruscan necropolises, monumental tombs, burial chambers carved into the rock, and the remains of Etruscan and Roman settlements.

    RV: The events in the novel occur in the early 1970s. Was there a particular reason for choosing this time period?

    According to recent reports, SN: Yes, there is. Choosing this period was an exciting challenge, and one that felt necessary. The Witch’s Mouth was born out of long conversations with tomb raiders and smugglers who were active during that time. Suddenly I came across some truly extraordinary, almost unbelievable stories. That’s when I began thinking about using this material as the basis for a novel.

    There were also three aspects that I found particularly fascinating. First of all, the “fever” I always noticed in the people who told me about their adventures. That’s the expression they would use: “digging fever.” It went beyond money or swashbuckling adventure—a special light would sparkle in their eyes. As these small-town Indiana Jones recalled those times, that almost addictive excitement was rekindled— the excitement of the moment when, after devising a plan, they would finally manage to break into a burial site, the first people to set foot there in millennia. And then reach out and touch the objects… Part of my job was to try to capture their passion.

    The second aspect was even more intriguing and had to do specifically with the Val di Cornia. The trafficking of archaeological artifacts was already underway in other parts of Italy—for instance in the Tuscia region—but in this small corner of Tuscany, people were late to the game.

    Sources indicate that I heard crazy stories of farmers whose cellars were filled with bronzes that had turned up when they were plowing the land, and who would give them to their grandchildren to play with, like toy soldiers. After storms at sea, amphorae would wash up on the shore at Baratti. Kids would place them on top of low walls and throw rocks at them. Women would show up at Mass on Sunday wearing earrings and necklaces found in the fields….

    So I wondered, what would happen if an entire community, largely made up of people who struggle to make ends meet, suddenly realized that their homes were full of objects they considered worthless but that could fetch millions on the black market?

    As I was researching the historical archives of the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, I came across a news story from 1971 about a twelve-inch bronze artifact seized by the Carabinieri. It was about to be sold to an American collector for half a billion lire (roughly $5 million in today’s money). People in that region had piles of similar bronzes, tossed aside in a corner.

    Finally, a purely personal aspect. I spent part of my childhood and adolescence in that region. Other kids and I would form our own little gangs and sneak out of the house in the middle of the night armed, with ropes, shovels, and spades, and head off into the woods. We imagined we were living in The Goonies, but instead of searching for One-Eyed Willy’s treasure, we were searching for Etruscan artifacts. Thinking back on it, what mattered wasn’t so much finding something as the adventure itself. Entering the woods at night was a big challenge. And then the thrill of digging, without really knowing where to look… In a way, I think I experienced some of that same fever the “professional” tomb raiders talked about.

    RV: The Witch’s Mouth is an ensemble novel with a lot of different characters, but it revolves around Bardo. He’s almost a godfather-type figure in the way he involves so many different kinds of people in his activities and spreads the wealth he earns. Tell us about your inspiration for creating him.

    SN: Everything that happens in the novel is inspired by the interviews I mentioned earlier. But the characters are entirely the product of my imagination, as are the main plot and the various subplots.

    In a recent development, when it comes to Bardo, I did a little “plundering” myself. Based on the stories I heard, I imagined this guy who, even as a kid, recognized the value of these artifacts, which everyone else treated like useless old junk taking up space.

    But Bardo is also a man of action, and a pretty clever one. He knows how hard life is for the families of Populonia. He starts getting them to hand over their “pieces,” as they call them in the trade, and then sells them to the more experienced tomb raiders in the Tuscia region, returning with the money. Real money, not a few pennies.

    Industry observers note that before long, everyone starts looking at Bardo like a sort of saint. Everyone is knocking on his door with an artifact in their hand. And Bardo is extremely good at weaving a network built on trust and gratitude. That means protection—Bardo is untouchable. This is something else that fascinated me: at least in the beginning, there wasn’t a gun in sight. But then the operation grows exponentially. Billions of lire start pouring in. And where there’s that much money, guns usually follow.

    In a recent development, RV: Of the novel’s many great characters, I was fascinated by Elisa, Bardo’s wife; Silvana, the prostitute; and the Marquis. As you write, do you have favorites? Do some of the characters come more easily to you than others?

    SN: Obviously I love them all, not only because of the role they each play in the story—a character is always an opportunity to explore different points of view, different lives and legacies… What I mean is, how does a particular character, with their own history, react to certain events? That’s part of the magic of writing. Especially when we explore uncomfortable aspects of human nature and relationships.

    According to recent reports, that remarked, among the characters you mentioned, Silvana and the Marchese have a special place in my heart. Silvana truly is the queen (I should say, the Principessa) of the novel. The Marchese, for his part, embodies a desperation that is part of the landscape and is compounded by his broken dreams, a desperation that still moves me. Although in the end… but I’d better stop here.

    RV: In many ways, this is the story of a gang of tomb robbers but it’s also the story of an ecosystem of stolen goods and people.

    Industry observers note that SN: I had some interesting experiences in this respect during the promotion of the book in Italy. Together with my Italian publishers, we had the wonderful idea of organizing some events in archaeological museums. Some of the events were fantastic. In other cases, though, for instance in Vetulonia, the director of the magnificent local museum declined to participate. He didn’t want to celebrate, right in a place designed to house Etruscan artifacts, a story about thieves who had deprived everyone of the opportunity to admire works of art and experience the sense of connection we can feel with the people who lived in distant times.

    But I’m not an educator; I’m a novelist. I try to make sense of the world through stories. Even if these stories are unsettling—in fact, all the better. What I’m saying is, “Hey, look, this happened too.” I’m saying, “Hey, look at how these people lived. How they reacted, what they dreamt about, what circumstances led them to make certain choices.” And I know very well that it’s wrong to prevent the public from viewing a work of art, locking it away instead in some billionaire’s safe.

    I’ll go further. For me, the real damage inflicted by tomb raiders is not the sale of a particular artifact to a private collector. The real theft—and maybe it’s the novelist in me talking—has to do with removing a clue (the artifact itself) from the place where it was found, thereby interrupting a story. Otherwise, archaeologists would be able to tell us how people loved, what clothes they wore or what food they ate, what gods they worshipped, what stories they passed down in that very place. This is what they rob us of, to make a few million dollars. I hope that somehow, between the lines of my novel, this message comes across. But according to some museum directors, I’ve missed the mark.

    RV: Are there other novels or writers you draw inspiration from in your work?

    SN: The list would be endless, stretching from my formative years to the present, now that I’ve just turned fifty. It would comprise all the different kinds of writing I’ve sought out, explored, and measured myself against. And yet I feel like I’m just starting out.

    Industry observers note that to mention some writers that have a place in my heart, in no particular order: Italo Calvino, Stephen King, Albert Camus, Joyce Carol Oates, John Steinbeck, Chuck Palahniuk, Beppe Fenoglio, Ágota Kristóf, Mikhail Bulgakov. If you asked me again a minute from now, the list would be completely different. I’m thinking of John Fante, or the fantasy novels I adored as a teenager. And what about Dumas and his Count of Monte Cristo?

    Seriously, I never know how to answer this question. But I think that each of these writers has given me a great gift: they “gave me permission” to be brave. To let my imagination spill onto the page, for what it’s worth. And all the voices that come with it.

    RV: What are you reading and/or working on at the moment?

    SN: On my nightstand are books by David Szalay and Ernest Jünger—the latter a special gift I received, a book that I’ve already read but want to reread. Recently, I returned to John Fante’s Wait Until Spring, Bandini after many years—what a knockout. I don’t think it will ever get old. I also really loved Tiffany McDaniel’s The Summer That Melted Everything.

    It has been revealed that on my computer is a novel forthcoming in Italy, Il ronzio (“The Buzzing”), which is in the final stages of editing. Of course, I’m also working on another novel. And I’m having fun writing the treatment for a TV series, which is due soon. And listen to this: after twenty years of writing books, for the first time ever, there’s a police inspector in one of my stories. I never would have imagined it.

    Radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The Latest York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

    Medieval Settings Are Back In These Mysteries, Thrillers, and Horror Novels

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that there’s a whole latest wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases.
    • Note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting.
    • Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that there’s a whole latest wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases. Before I get to the recommendations, you may be wondering: what time period exactly are we talking? For the purposes of this article, the medieval era is roughly defined as between 1000-1500, depending on where the characters live. For example: 15th century Italy = Renaissance. 15th century Estonia = Medieval. Burgundy, I suppose, is half and half. Periodization is a continuum much more than a series of hard stops and new beginnings, and the Renaissance is just the Middle Ages with better marketing (see Inventing the Renaissance for more on the debate).

    Note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting. Most are upcoming releases from this year or next year, but there are two older titles that are still recent enough to count for this trend. Books that are not yet published have their publication dates next to their publisher info. If you’ve got any Dark Ages-set mysteries to recommend to me, please comment, because I would very much like to read them.

    In a recent development, M. T. Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.

    Industry observers note that this came out in 2024, which I consider recent enough to include as part of this trend piece—especially when considering a medieval time scale. Also it’s awesome. In Nicked, a group of disparate travelers sets off on an odyssey of the medieval world with a common 11th century mission: they’ve been hired to steal the Anatolian relics of a powerful saint and transport them to an Italian city state in hopes of sparking more commerce from pilgrims (the medieval equivalent of taking the Dodgers from Brooklyn to LA). Along the way, they form deep bonds, some blossoming into romance, and take in the sights and sounds of the entire Mediterranean world. M. T. Anderson does that rare feat of capturing the spirit of the time, granting readers a lively, Rabelaisian interpretation of an unfairly maligned era (see history book The Bright Ages for further appreciation).

    Paul Brous, The Undying Lamb (Rising Action) Setting: Italian states, 1230.

    Industry observers note that when a book starts with a glossary featuring words from several now-dead languages, you just know that it’s going to be impeccably researched. In Paul Brous’ medieval-set thriller, an Albigensian assassin and an English knight must protect a child with an inconvenient lineage, as a vast array of forces attempt to eliminate their vulnerable charge. Perfect for those who enjoyed Conclave, but wish it had been set waaaay further back in history.

    James Bennett, Mother of Night (Evil Twin, March 2027) Setting: Holy Roman Empire, 1291.

    According to recent reports, in this intense work of historical horror, Saladin’s victories have sent a ragged group of crusaders fleeing from the Holy Land, their only option to board a rickety vessel soon enough broken by stormy seas. Shipwrecked and far from home, the few survivors find succor and strangeness amongst a group of miserable swamp-dwellers who warn of danger ahead; the crusaders, determined to forge ahead, do not listen, with predictably dire consequences and a surprising amount of singing.

    Ferdia Lennon, Brother Nothing (Holt, June 2027) Setting: France, 1369.

    According to recent reports, set just a decade before the events of Doom Painting, Brother Nothing follows a newly appointed provost and his precociously intelligent daughter as they flee plague-ridden Paris for a town in the North of France. While their latest abode does appear safe from pestilence, other dangers are many, including the perennial threat of English soldiers, an epidemic of children gone missing, and a murder pinned on a prodigal son who confesses to every possible crime— save the crime of which he is accused. As the provost uncovers layer after layer of shocking crimes and terrifying cover-ups, he and his few allies begin to suspect the entire town of conspiracy, for what reads a bit like Red Harvest, medieval style.

    A.K. Blakemore, Doom Painting (Scribner, April 2027) Setting: England, 1381.

    I have complete trust in A.K. Blakemore’s power to render historical fiction as vivid and complex as depictions of the present, and her newly introduced novel of the English Peasant’s Revolt does not disappoint. In 1381, England’s most oppressed rose up against the conditions of their serfdom, driven to rebellion by the devastation of the plague and the endless war with France. For 16 days, they challenged the notion that some should rule while others serve, embodied by Wat Tyler’s epic call-to-arms: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then a gentleman?” As a side note, I’ve been planning to get a tattoo of that slogan in Ye Olde Englishe font for a while now, so maybe it’s time to bite the bullet. Also the book confirms what I have always known: Wat Tyler had major sex appeal.

    Indrek Hargla, The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press) Setting: 15th Century Tallinn.

    It has been revealed that indrek Hargla’s tale of a crime-solving apothecary is based in obscure, and very real, history; the mystery unraveled by the amateur sleuth takes its jumping off point from a mysterious note in Latvian historical records, for a richly detailed and vividly imagined take on a high-water mark in Latvia’s regional influence. In The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church, the murder of an aging knight leads a city luminary towards a horrifying secret with deep implications for the city’s fragile economic status and unstable power structure.

    Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street (Pushkin Press) Setting: Estonia, 1419.

    Hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

    Jo Harkin, The Pretender Setting: England, Ireland, Burgundy, 15th Century.

    At the tail end of the Wars of the Roses, an ordinary farm boy is plucked from his simple village life and trained up to become a king. He’s been swapped for a commoner at birth by his dead Earl of a father and forgotten about in the midst of internecine warfare; now, he’s the last hope for the house of York to triumph over its Tudor rivals. But does he have the stuff it takes to fight through his own doubts and become king? And will he survive the endless sacrifices demanded in his ascent to the throne? This is an excellent book to help you understand the inspirations behind Game of Thrones, or the power politics of Elaine’s kingdom in Wheel of Time.

    Katherine Arden, The Unicorn Hunter (Del Rey) Setting: Brittany, Late 15th Century.

    According to recent reports, in 15th century Brittany, a noblewoman facing an unwanted union with a far-away lord puts in motion a clever plan to hold off the wedding: her husband-to-be must join her in a unicorn hunt in the dense, dark forest near to her castle. Soon, they find themselves transported into a magical realm beset by an ancient curse that only the lady and her wooing courtiers can break. The Unicorn Hunter takes its inspiration from the real Anne of Brittany, whose marriage to the King of France was just another method of preserving what little sovereignty her province could hold onto under the steady creep of French imperial influence, and who brought two beds to her wedding as a symbol of her independence. I think I would have quite liked Anne of Brittany—Katharine Arden certainly feels a sprightly kinship with the impish aristocrat.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, as longtime CrimeReads readers (“CrimeReaders”) know, the editors of this website are always interested in news related to the Loch Ness Monster. Especially me. For example, several years ago, I wrote about how, in 2016, a bunch of Norwegian scientists had sent a high-tech robot down into Loch Ness to scan the, and the robot sent back sonar scans of a creature that looked exactly like the Loch Ness monster, but actually, it turned out to be a model of the Loch Ness Monster built for the 1969 film The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes that had accidentally sunk during filming. So that was a bummer. A HILARIOUS bummer, but a bummer nonetheless.

    Sources indicate that any Loch Ness Monster-related news intrigues me. So you can imagine my delight when I came across news of an upcoming series from the BBC and BritBox. It’s called The Loch Ness Mysteries.

    It’s set near Loch Ness, obviously, and it’s about a young, irascible, beautiful London detective who winds up being kicked out (I think?) of her job, only to wind up investigating a personal matter near Inverness… and being drawn into a strange mystery near Loch Ness.

    So, in the words of the genius who wrote the BBC’s press release, “from Scotland Yard to Scotland Scotland.”.

    Also, what’s the beautiful, brilliant, difficult detective’s name? DCI Vanessa “Nessie” Keen.

    It has been revealed that the series will star Melissa George, Jamie Sives, and Ashley Storrie, and will be six episodes long. Ed Sellek of Sister Boniface Mysteries is the creator and head writer.

    Filming begins before the end of the year, so stay tuned!
